Going to try to overestimate here...

1 inch of water running down the 6 inch wide sleuce. At best, the water is moving at 3 feet per second. We'll round up and say he's got 1 gallon per second flowing in. Looks like maybe 3 feet of head. At 100% efficiency, if you could capture all of the potential energy of the water and convert it into usable electricity, that would be 32.4 watts. So, this couldn't keep up with a standard light bulb.

A 100 watt solar panel can be had for about 120 bucks without much shopping, but it is only collecting power when the sun is out, and this thing is running 24x7.

That's about 784.8 watt-hours. It would take 3 days to fully charge a car battery off of this if you had 100% efficiency. Which... again... obviously, you don't. And that car battery would be totally flat after running a single light bulb through the night.

I have a similar stream and was sad to find out I really couldn't get much usable power out of it.

The indicator on his battery is showing the battery voltage, which is at a charging voltage. So he is charging the batteries, yay.

His battery bank of 5 batteries would take around 18 days to charge (Again, under 100% efficiency for all of these conversions, which, no), though actually less because they're all dead freebies that won't hold that much charge. And of course they'll discharge under ~5 night's use of a single bulb.

This is a case of an interesting hobby, and a dude who can cobble some cheap/free stuff together to get some use out of it... but you could probably spend less money on a smaller off the shelf system and have a simpler, more reliable system with greater power capacity. you could power several standard LED light bulbs with 20watts. looks like he can make lighting for his entire house for 20 bucks or whatever he spent on this project. he could definitely make easy changes to his setup and get double the power out of it. like increase the head.
